subject: Medicine
summary: Blood grouping identifies ABO and Rh antigens to ensure safe transfusion, transplantation, and pregnancy management. Cross‑matching adds compatibility testing for other blood proteins. Errors can be fatal, so accurate typing is critical.

sections.p: Blood grouping determines the presence or absence of A, B, and Rh(D) antigens on red cells using serologic reactions. Diagnosis is made by forward (cell) and reverse (serum) typing.
b: Forward typing: patient red cells + anti‑A, anti‑B, anti‑D reagents.
Reverse typing: patient serum + known A and B cells.

t.b: What antigens are on the patient’s red cells? Positive reaction indicates presence of that antigen.
What antibodies are in the patient’s plasma? Positive reaction confirms absence of the corresponding antigen.
Is the D antigen present? Determines Rh‑positive vs. Rh‑negative status.

sections.p: Blood grouping itself is not a disease, but mismatched transfusion can cause hemolytic reactions graded by severity (mild, moderate, severe, fatal).

Incorrect typing arises from technical errors, weak subgroups, or recent transfusion. In low‑resource settings, high prevalence of alloantibodies from malaria or sickle‑cell transfusions adds complexity.
b: Weak A or B subgroups (e.g., A2).

sections.p: Patients are usually asymptomatic; problems appear only when a mismatched blood product is given, leading to acute hemolytic transfusion reaction or delayed hemolysis.
b: Acute reaction: pain, hypotension within minutes.
Delayed reaction: anemia, jaundice 3‑10 days later.

sections.p: Beyond basic typing, extended phenotyping and antibody screening are used when a patient has a history of transfusion or pregnancy.

t.b: Are there clinically significant alloantibodies? Positive result requires identification before transfusion.
What additional antigens are present? Guides matched blood for chronically transfused patients.
What is the genotype when serology is inconclusive? Useful when reagents unavailable.

sections.p: A mismatch can cause life‑threatening hemolysis, renal failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or death.
Stop the transfusion immediately, support circulation, and treat hemolysis. Use compatible blood after repeat typing and antibody identification.
b: IV fluids and diuretics to protect kidneys.
Consider plasma exchange for severe reactions.

sections.p: Document the confirmed blood type and any antibodies in the patient’s record. Use pre‑transfusion testing for every future transfusion.
b: Educate patients about their blood type.

sections.p: Cross‑matching, which tests compatibility beyond ABO/Rh, and antibody screening, which looks for unexpected antibodies.
b: Cross‑match: checks for agglutination between donor cells and recipient serum.
Antibody screen: detects alloantibodies that may cause delayed reactions.

sections.p: Recent transfusion can mask the true ABO type (mixed-field reactions). Weak subgroups may give false‑negative reactions.
b: A2 subgroup may be misread as O.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction with hypotension, dark urine, or chest pain.
Delayed hemolysis causing severe anemia or jaundice.

faq.q: Why is Rh typing important in pregnancy?
faq.a: An Rh‑negative mother can develop anti‑D antibodies that destroy an Rh‑positive fetus’s red cells, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn.

faq.q: Can a person have more than one ABO type?
faq.a: No, each individual has a single ABO phenotype, but recent transfusion can create a mixed‑field pattern that mimics multiple types.

faq.q: What is the difference between blood grouping and cross‑matching?
faq.a: Blood grouping identifies ABO/Rh antigens; cross‑matching tests donor red cells against recipient serum for all other clinically relevant antibodies.

exam: Explain how forward and reverse typing confirm a patient’s ABO group.
Describe the steps to manage an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
List three reasons why a blood group result might be inaccurate.
